delivery_fee.title: A small parcel fee with a big rush

cards.heading: Pause before paying
cards.body: An unexpected text asking for a small redelivery fee may be a scam, especially if it gives you only minutes to act.

cards.heading: Check the link
cards.body: A strange-looking link can lead to a fake payment page designed to collect your card details.

cards.heading: Check another way
cards.body: Don’t tap the text link. Open the delivery company’s app or website yourself to check whether a fee is really due.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this text should make you pause?

message.text: Your parcel is waiting. Pay a $1.20 redelivery fee within 30 minutes: swiftparcel-track.example

flags.why: The short deadline pressures you to act without checking.
An unexpected, unfamiliar link may lead to a fake payment page.

quiz.explain: Scammers may use a small fee and a short deadline to rush you into sharing card details.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t tap the link. Check the delivery in the company’s app or website, opened separately.

quiz.prompt: You get an unexpected text asking for a small redelivery fee. What’s the safest next step?
options: Tap the link and pay before the deadline
Open the delivery company’s app or website yourself to check
Reply with your card details
quiz.explain: A deadline in an unexpected text is a reason to pause, not rush.
quiz.safe_action: Open the company’s app or website yourself and check whether a fee is due.

quiz.prompt: Is this text real or a scam?

message.text: Pay a small redelivery fee now using this link, or your parcel will be returned today.

quiz.explain: The threat of losing the parcel and the push to pay now are warning signs.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t use the link. Check your parcel through the delivery company’s app or website.

bank_impersonation.title: A “safe account” call may be a scam

cards.heading: A familiar-sounding caller
cards.body: A caller may claim to be from your bank’s fraud team. A confident voice or knowledge of your details does not prove they are genuine.

cards.heading: Watch for pressure
cards.body: Scammers may say your money is under attack and you must act now. Rushing you makes it harder to stop and check.

cards.heading: Keep your money and codes safe
cards.body: Don’t move money to a “safe account” or tell a caller a one-time code. Hang up, wait five minutes, and call the number on the back of your card.

quiz.prompt: A caller says they’re from your bank and tells you to move your savings to a safe account. What should you do?
options: Move the money before it is stolen
Hang up, wait five minutes, and call the number on your card
Ask the caller to prove who they are by sending a text
quiz.explain: A caller claiming to be from your bank does not prove they are genuine. The safe-account story is a warning sign.
quiz.safe_action: Hang up, wait five minutes, and call the number on the back of your card.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you pause?

message.text: We are from Northgate Bank's fraud team. Your account is under attack. Move your money to this safe account right now and read us the code we just sent.

flags.span: We are from Northgate Bank's fraud team.
flags.why: A caller’s claim to work for a bank is not proof of their identity.
This alarming claim can be used to frighten you into acting without checking.

flags.span: Move your money to this safe account right now
flags.why: Pressure to move money urgently is a serious warning sign.

flags.span: read us the code we just sent
flags.why: A genuine bank should not ask you to share a one-time code with a caller.

quiz.explain: The caller uses a bank identity and a frightening story to push you into moving money and sharing a code.
quiz.safe_action: Do not share the code or move money. Hang up, wait five minutes, and call the number on your card.

quiz.prompt: Is this call real or a scam?

message.text: This is Northgate Bank. We spotted a suspicious payment. Please hang up and call the number printed on the back of your bank card. We will never ask you to move money or tell us a code.

quiz.explain: The message does not ask you to share a code or move money. It directs you to contact the bank using a trusted number.
quiz.safe_action: Call the number on the back of your card yourself, rather than replying to the caller.

cards.heading: Big promises are a warning
cards.body: Crypto prices can rise or fall. No investment can honestly guarantee big returns. A promise of easy, certain profits is a reason to pause.

cards.heading: Check the recommendation
cards.body: A celebrity’s name or a friend’s recommendation doesn’t prove an investment is safe. People may be misled, or someone may be pretending to be them.

cards.heading: Check before paying
cards.body: Look up the firm yourself on the official financial regulator’s register before paying. If you can’t withdraw money, don’t send more to unlock it.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you pause?

message.text: Earn guaranteed 20% returns every month with our crypto platform. A famous investor recommends us. Pay today to secure your place.

flags.why: Investments can’t promise high returns with certainty.
A name or endorsement may be false and doesn’t prove the offer is safe.

flags.span: Pay today to secure your place
flags.why: Pressure to pay quickly can stop you from checking the firm.

quiz.explain: Guaranteed high returns and pressure to pay are strong warning signs. Check the firm independently before considering any investment.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t pay through the message. Find the firm on the official financial regulator’s register yourself.

quiz.prompt: A crypto platform says you must pay another fee before you can withdraw your money. What’s the safest next step?
options: Pay the fee so you can get your money back
Stop sending money and check the firm independently
Ask the person who recommended it to pay for you
quiz.explain: Being asked for more money to release a withdrawal can be part of a scam. Paying more may lead to further demands.
quiz.safe_action: Stop payments and contact your bank or payment provider using a number you find independently.

quiz.prompt: Is this offer real or a scam?

message.text: Your investment is guaranteed to double in 30 days. Send money now and we’ll handle everything.

quiz.explain: A guaranteed doubling of money is unrealistic, and the message pressures you to send money without checking the offer.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t send money. Check the firm on the official financial regulator’s register using contact details you find yourself.

romance.title: When an online partner asks for money

cards.heading: Strong feelings can come quickly
cards.body: Someone may say they love you before you have met. Warm words can feel real, but they don’t prove who is behind the messages.

cards.heading: Notice the pattern
cards.body: Be cautious if they always avoid video calls, describe an emergency, or ask you to pay for travel or medical bills.

cards.heading: Keep money matters open
cards.body: A request to keep the relationship or money private is a warning sign. Talk it through with someone you trust before doing anything.

cards.heading: Pause before sending
cards.body: Don’t send money to someone you haven’t met in person. Stop replying if you feel pressured, and ask a trusted person for support.

quiz.prompt: Someone you met online says they need money for travel and asks you not to tell anyone. What is the safest next step?
options: Send a small amount to see if they repay it
Keep it private and ask them for more details
Pause, don’t send money, and talk to someone you trust
quiz.explain: A request for money combined with secrecy is a serious warning sign, especially when you haven’t met in person.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t send money. Talk to a trusted friend or family member before replying.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you cautious?

message.text: I love you so much, even though we haven't met yet. I need money for a medical bill. Please keep this between us and don't video call—my camera is broken.

flags.span: I love you so much, even though we haven't met yet.
flags.why: Very strong feelings before meeting can be a warning sign.

flags.span: I need money for a medical bill.
flags.why: A request for money for an emergency is a common warning sign.
Asking you to keep the request secret can stop you getting helpful advice.

flags.span: don't video call—my camera is broken.
flags.why: Repeatedly avoiding a video call can make it harder to know who you’re talking to.

quiz.explain: The message combines secrecy, an emergency money request, intense feelings, and avoiding a video call.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t send money. Save the messages and discuss them with someone you trust.

quiz.prompt: Is this message safe to trust?

message.text: I enjoy chatting with you. I’m not comfortable asking you for money, and I’d be happy to video call when you’re ready.

quiz.explain: This message does not ask for money or secrecy, and it respects your choice about a video call. Still, take time to get to know someone online.
quiz.safe_action: Keep personal and financial details private, and talk to someone you trust if anything feels uncomfortable.

tech_support.title: A virus warning that wants control

cards.heading: A scary warning can be a trick
cards.body: An unexpected pop-up or caller may claim your computer has a virus to frighten you into acting quickly.

cards.heading: Don’t hand over control
cards.body: Never install an app or give a stranger remote access to “fix” your computer. They could see your files or use your accounts.

cards.heading: Pause and close it
cards.body: Close the page or hang up. If you’re worried, contact a trusted computer helper using details you find yourself.

quiz.prompt: A pop-up says your computer is infected and tells you to call a number. What’s the safest next step?
options: Call the number to check
Close the page without calling
Install the app it recommends
quiz.explain: An unexpected virus warning can use fear to push you into contacting a scammer.
quiz.safe_action: Close the page. If it won’t close, ask a trusted person for help.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you pause?

message.text: URGENT: Your computer has 7 viruses. Call 555-0148 now. Install FixNest and pay $249 so we can stop hackers.

flags.why: It tries to make you act before you can think.
A frightening claim from an unexpected message may be made up.
It directs you to contact a number supplied in the warning.
It asks you to install an app and pay a stranger.

quiz.explain: The message uses a scary virus claim and pressure to get access and money.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t call, install the app, or pay. Close the message and ask a trusted computer helper if you’re concerned.

quiz.prompt: Is this likely real or a scam?

message.text: Your files are at risk. Let us control your computer now to remove a virus.

quiz.explain: The unexpected warning uses fear and asks for remote control of your computer.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t allow access. Close the page or hang up, then contact a trusted helper using details you find yourself.

cards.heading: A code is a key
cards.body: A one-time code can let someone into your account. Keep it private, even if the person asking sounds helpful.

cards.heading: Watch for a change of channel
cards.body: A message or caller may say a code was sent by mistake, then ask you to read it out. That request is a warning sign.

cards.heading: Check for yourself
cards.body: Don’t reply or share the code. Open the service’s app yourself or use contact details you already trust to check your account.

quiz.prompt: You receive a one-time code you didn’t request. Someone then calls and asks you to read it out. What should you do?
options: Read it out if they say it was sent by mistake
Keep it private and check your account using the service’s app or trusted contact details
Send it by text instead
quiz.explain: The caller is moving from an unexpected code to a request for the code. Sharing it could give them access to your account.
quiz.safe_action: End the call, keep the code private, and open the service’s app yourself to check your account.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you pause?

message.text: Your sign-in code was sent by mistake. Please read the code to our agent on this call so we can cancel it.

flags.why: This may be a story to make an unexpected code seem harmless.

flags.span: read the code to our agent on this call
flags.why: A one-time code should not be shared with someone who contacts you.

quiz.explain: The message turns an unexpected code into a reason to speak with an agent and hand it over. A familiar-looking name doesn’t prove the request is genuine.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t share the code. End the call and check your account through the service’s app or trusted contact details.

quiz.prompt: Is this message safe to follow?

message.text: Your delivery needs an address check. Reply with the sign-in code you just received so we can confirm your account.

quiz.explain: A delivery message is asking for a sign-in code, which could give someone access to your account. Don’t share one-time codes.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t reply. Check delivery details using the parcel service’s app or website that you open yourself.

job_task.title: A job that asks you to pay

cards.heading: A surprise offer
cards.body: Be cautious if a job offer arrives when you never applied. A friendly message or simple task doesn’t prove the job is genuine.

cards.heading: Likes for money?
cards.body: Scammers may promise easy pay for liking or rating posts. The offer can sound tempting, but the earnings may be fake.

cards.heading: Pay to unlock earnings
cards.body: A request to pay a deposit or fee before you can get paid is a major warning sign. Don’t send money to work.

cards.heading: Pause and protect yourself
cards.body: Stop replying and block the contact. If you’re unsure, check the company using contact details you find independently.

quiz.prompt: A stranger offers you money for rating posts. What should make you most cautious?
options: They ask you to pay a deposit to receive your earnings
They explain what the task involves
They give you time to think
quiz.explain: A demand for money before you can get paid is a strong warning sign, even if the task sounds simple.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t pay. Stop replying and block the contact.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message are warning signs?

message.text: Earn $180 today by liking posts. Pay a $25 deposit to unlock your earnings. Reply in 10 minutes to claim your spot.

flags.why: Easy money for simple online tasks can be bait.

flags.span: Pay a $25 deposit to unlock your earnings.
flags.why: A job should not require you to pay to receive your wages.
A short deadline pressures you to act without checking.

quiz.explain: The message promises easy earnings, asks for money, and rushes you. Together, these are strong scam signs.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t send money or reply. Block the contact.

quiz.prompt: Is this offer real or a scam?

message.text: We’ll pay you to rate posts. To withdraw your first earnings, send a deposit. You can earn more after that.

quiz.explain: The promise of pay is used to lure you in, but the deposit request is the key warning sign.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t send a deposit. Stop replying and block the contact.

marketplace_purchase.title: Keep marketplace payments on the site

cards.heading: Use the site’s checkout
cards.body: Pay through the marketplace’s own checkout. It may offer protection if an order goes wrong.

cards.heading: A bargain can be bait
cards.body: A price far below similar listings is a reason to pause and check carefully.

cards.heading: Keep the chat there, too
cards.body: A seller who moves you off the marketplace may be trying to avoid its safety checks.

quiz.prompt: A seller asks you to pay by bank transfer instead of using the marketplace checkout. What should you do?
options: Pay if the seller seems friendly
Use the marketplace’s checkout or leave the deal
Send a small amount first
quiz.explain: A bank transfer may be hard to get back, and paying outside the site can remove marketplace protection.
quiz.safe_action: Use the marketplace’s own checkout, or stop the purchase.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this seller’s message are warning signs?

message.text: This is half the usual price. Send a bank transfer today and message me off PineCart to arrange it.

flags.why: A price far below similar listings can be bait.
A bank transfer may be difficult to recover, and ‘today’ adds pressure.
Moving the conversation away from the marketplace can bypass its safety tools.

quiz.explain: The message combines an unusually low price, pressure, an unsafe payment method, and a request to leave the marketplace.
quiz.safe_action: Do not pay or move the chat. Use the site’s checkout and reporting tools.

quiz.prompt: Is this seller’s request safe or a scam warning?

message.text: The checkout is broken. Transfer the money to me directly and I’ll send the item.

quiz.explain: The seller wants you to pay outside the marketplace, where you may lose its protection.
quiz.safe_action: Only pay through the marketplace’s own checkout. If it is not working, wait or choose another listing.

cards.heading: A familiar name, a new number
cards.body: A message may sound like it comes from a family member, but arrive from a number you don’t know. Don’t rely on the name or story alone.

cards.heading: Pressure and secrecy
cards.body: A request for money today, especially with “don’t tell anyone” or “I can’t talk,” can stop you checking. Take a moment before doing anything.

cards.heading: Check another way
cards.body: Call your family member on the number you already have. You can also ask a question only they would know.

cards.heading: Keep control of your money
cards.body: Don’t send money to a new or unfamiliar account just because a message says it’s urgent. Speak with someone you trust first.

quiz.prompt: A new number says your family member needs money today and asks you not to tell anyone. What is the safest first step?
options: Send a small amount to help quickly
Call them on the number you already have
Reply asking for their new account details
quiz.explain: A request to keep things secret can stop you getting help or checking the story. Verify with your family member another way.
quiz.safe_action: Call your family member on their old number before sending any money.

quiz.prompt: What would you make of this message?

message.text: Hi Mum, it's me. I lost my phone. I can't talk on the phone. Please don't tell anyone yet. I need money today—send it to this new account.

quiz.explain: The sender uses a new number, avoids a phone call, asks for secrecy, and wants money sent urgently to an unfamiliar account.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t send money. Call your family member using the number you already have.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you pause?

message.text: Hi Mum, I lost my phone. I can't talk on the phone. Please don't tell anyone yet. I need money today—send it to this new account.

flags.span: I can't talk on the phone.
flags.why: It gets in the way of checking who is really messaging you.
Secrecy can stop you asking someone you trust for help.
The rush may pressure you into acting before you check.

flags.span: send it to this new account
flags.why: The account is unfamiliar, so verify the request before paying.

quiz.explain: These details together are warning signs. A real family emergency can still be checked through a trusted number.
quiz.safe_action: Call your family member on their old number, or ask a question only they would know.

cards.heading: A refund you weren’t expecting?
cards.body: A message promising money back can feel like a pleasant surprise. Pause before you act, especially if you weren’t expecting a refund.

cards.heading: Don’t follow the link
cards.body: A link in an unexpected refund message could lead to a fake page. Don’t tap it or enter personal or payment details.

cards.heading: Keep your bank details private
cards.body: You shouldn’t need to share your bank login or card details to claim a refund through a message link.

cards.heading: Check for yourself
cards.body: Close the message and visit your tax service using an address you already know or find independently. If unsure, ask someone you trust to help check.

quiz.prompt: Which parts of this message should make you pause?

message.text: You have a tax refund waiting. Claim your $420 today at claim-refund.example and enter your bank login to receive it.

flags.span: You have a tax refund waiting.
flags.why: An unexpected refund can be tempting. Check independently before taking action.
It urges you to use a message link to claim money.
Never share your bank login to receive a refund.

quiz.explain: The promise of unexpected money is being used to draw you into a link that asks for sensitive details.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t use the link. Visit your tax service using an address you know, or find its contact details independently.

quiz.prompt: You get a text about a refund you weren’t expecting. What’s the safest next step?
options: Tap the link, but only enter your details if the page looks official
Reply asking whether the refund is real
Ignore the link and check through your tax service independently
quiz.explain: A convincing-looking page or reply may still be part of a scam. Checking separately avoids relying on the message.
quiz.safe_action: Open your tax service using an address you already know or find independently.

quiz.prompt: Is this message real or a scam?

message.text: A refund is ready for you. Use this link to claim it and enter your card details.

quiz.explain: It promises money and asks you to use a link and provide card details. Treat unexpected refund messages cautiously.
quiz.safe_action: Don’t tap the link or share card details. Check with your tax service using independently found contact details.
